newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Anti-Taleban forces launch attacks north of Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Anti-Taleban forces launch attacks north of Kabul.

text.p: Opposition forces launched fresh attacks on the Taleban militia and its allies north of Kabul on Thursday, a Pakistan-based news agency reported.

The Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) said fighters loyal to former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood had begun an offensive against Taleban positions on the outskirts of Jabal os-Siraj, about 70 km (44 miles) north of Kabul.

The two sides battled for at least two hours, using artillery and rockets, but there was no word on whether any ground had changed hands in the town, strategically located on the main highway linking the Afghan capital with the north.
Masood's men control most of Jabal os-Siraj, but Taleban fighters hold a sprawling Soviet-built army base and some other buildings in its southern outskirts, AIP said.
It quoted Taleban officials as saying that at least five Taleban fighters had been wounded in the clashes, but there was no word on opposition casualties.
Further north, Shi'ite Moslem and Ismaili opposition militias renewed their attacks on Hizb-i-Islami fighters loyal to Bashir Baghlani, who holds the town of Baghlan.

Forces of the Shi'ite Hezb-i-Wahdat militia and an Ismaili militia commanded by Syed Jafar Naderi launched an assault on Thursday from the town of Pul-i-Khumri towards Baghlan, about 30 km (19 miles) to the north, but made no progress, AIP said.
The Taleban repelled a similar offensive against Baghlan, in which opposition jets took part, on Wednesday, the agency said.
An estimated 3,000 Taleban fighters arrived in Baghlan last week after opposition attacks forced them out of Pul-i-Khumri.
Opposition spokesmen had said earlier that Baghlani had agreed to disarm and hand over the Taleban fighters to opposition forces, but he apparently joined them instead.
The latest fighting followed Tuesday's capture of the city of Kunduz, about 250 km (160 miles) north of Kabul, by the mainly ethnic Pashtun Taleban and allied local commanders.
Taleban officials said on Wednesday 90 percent of Kunduz province, important for its link with neighbouring Tajikistan, was now held by the purist Islamic militia and its allies.
The Taleban have vowed to impose strict Islamic rule across Afghanistan, a goal which their ethnic minority opponents in the north see as concealing a drive for Pashtun hegemony.
